title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Direct detection. Antigen detection (immunofluorescence, immunoperoxidase, EIA, rapid lateral-flow tests) or nucleic acid detection (PCR).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antibody classes. IgM appears after 7-14 days and indicates recent infection; IgG appears after 10-14 days and may persist for life.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Indirect diagnosis. Serology shows the host antibody response: specific IgM, or a significant rise in IgG.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Virus isolation. Cell culture is the historical gold standard: specimens are inoculated and cytopathic effect is observed over days to weeks.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Real-time PCR. Fluorescence is read every cycle; the Ct (threshold cycle) is inversely proportional to the amount of target: low Ct = high viral load.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Specimen. The most important step: the right specimen taken early, labelled with onset date and clinical signs, transported quickly at 4 °C (freezing destroys enveloped viruses).

title: Three approaches to viral diagnosis?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Three approaches to viral diagnosis?
body.back: Isolation (culture), direct (antigen, genome, EM), indirect (serology).

title: Specimen rules?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Specimen rules?
body.back: Right specimen, right time (early), rapid transport at 4 °C, not frozen; complete form.

title: What is CPE?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is CPE?
body.back: Cytopathic effect: visible changes in cultured cells due to the virus.

title: PCR steps and temperatures?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: PCR steps and temperatures?
body.back: Denaturation 94-98 °C, annealing 50-60 °C, extension 72 °C.

title: Ct value meaning?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Ct value meaning?
body.back: Cycle at which fluorescence crosses threshold; inversely proportional to viral load.

title: IgM vs IgG?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: IgM vs IgG?
body.back: IgM (7-14 days): recent. IgG (10-14 days on, lifelong): past/immunity; rise = recent.

title: Uses of sequencing?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Uses of sequencing?
body.back: Drug resistance, genotyping, epidemiology, evolution.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Norovirus. Caliciviridae; naked, positive-sense RNA; at least 7 genogroups, GII.4 dominant and changing every 2-3 years.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Norovirus control. No licensed vaccine (mRNA candidates in trials); relies on hygiene, bleach disinfection and isolation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Norovirus disease. The first cause of epidemic diarrhoea at all ages (85-90% of viral outbreaks) and of most hospital-acquired diarrhoea.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Management. No specific antiviral: rehydration, mostly oral, is the treatment.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rotavirus. Reoviridae; naked, double-stranded RNA in 11 segments; outer proteins VP7 (G type) and VP4 (P type) induce neutralising antibodies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rotavirus vaccines. Oral vaccines (attenuated or reassortant) protect against severe disease (>90%) but do not prevent all infection.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rotavirus disease. The most common cause of acute diarrhoea in children under 5: about 200,000 deaths a year and 30-65% of hospitalised diarrhoea; winter peaks.

title: Main gastroenteritis viruses?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Main gastroenteritis viruses?
body.back: Rotavirus, norovirus, sapovirus, adenovirus 40/41, astrovirus.

title: Rotavirus features?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Rotavirus features?
body.back: Reoviridae, dsRNA 11 segments, VP7 (G), VP4 (P); children < 5; winter.

title: Norovirus features?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Norovirus features?
body.back: Caliciviridae, (+)ssRNA, GII.4 dominant; outbreaks at all ages, nosocomial.

title: Disinfection against naked viruses?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Disinfection against naked viruses?
body.back: Bleach, iodine, peracetic acid, glutaraldehyde; handwashing with soap; alcohol less reliable.

title: Rotavirus vaccine?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Rotavirus vaccine?
body.back: Oral, attenuated or reassortant; 90-96% vs severe disease.

title: Treatment?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Treatment?
body.back: Rehydration; no antiviral.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HBe. Mutually exclusive with HBeAg; usually a low-replication phase (except with pre-core mutants).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HBs. Neutralising antibody: recovery from infection, or the only marker after vaccination.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: HBV DNA. Most accurate measure of replication; used to decide and monitor treatment.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: HBeAg. Marker of active replication and usually high viral load (≥10,000 IU/mL); high infectivity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: HBsAg. Surface antigen: marks current infection; persistence beyond 6 months defines chronic hepatitis B.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HBc IgG. The main marker of contact with HBV, whether resolved or chronic; absent after vaccination alone.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-HBc IgM. Marker of acute (recent) infection; useful in the window period when HBsAg has gone and anti-HBs is not yet detectable.

title: Enteric vs parenteral hepatitis viruses?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Enteric vs parenteral hepatitis viruses?
body.back: Enteric: A, E. Parenteral: B, C, D.

title: HAV serology?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HAV serology?
body.back: IgM+ = acute; IgG+ IgM− = past/immune.

title: Risk groups for severe HEV?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Risk groups for severe HEV?
body.back: Pregnant women (acute failure); immunocompromised (chronic).

title: Seven HBV markers?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Seven HBV markers?
body.back: HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HBc IgG, HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA.

title: HBV chronicity by age?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HBV chronicity by age?
body.back: Adults ~5%; infants 80-95%.

title: Co-infection vs superinfection with HDV?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Co-infection vs superinfection with HDV?
body.back: Co-infection: severe acute, rarely chronic. Superinfection: usually chronic, severe.

title: HCV testing sequence?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HCV testing sequence?
body.back: Anti-HCV → if reactive, HCV RNA: detected = current infection.

title: HBV cure definitions?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HBV cure definitions?
body.back: Sterilising, functional (HBsAg loss), partial (DNA undetectable, HBsAg present).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Treatment limit. Nucleoside analogues block viral DNA polymerase, so they treat episodes but cannot clear latent virus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neural spread. HSV and VZV reach the sensory ganglion supplying the site: trigeminal after oral infection, sacral after genital infection, dorsal root for VZV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Latency. The viral DNA persists for life as an episome in the neuron nucleus, without replication or protein expression, hidden from immunity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary infection. Usually limited to skin and mucous membranes; HSV-1 mostly in childhood (oral), HSV-2 mostly sexual (genital).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reactivation. Virus travels back along the nerve: cold sores, recurrent genital herpes, or shingles for VZV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Triggers. Stress, immunosuppression, UV light, fever or menstruation can reactivate the virus.

title: Herpesvirus structure?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Herpesvirus structure?
body.back: Large dsDNA, icosahedral capsid, envelope; nuclear replication.

title: Latency sites by subfamily?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Latency sites by subfamily?
body.back: α (HSV, VZV): sensory ganglia. β (CMV, HHV-6/7): glands, blood, kidney. γ (EBV, HHV-8): lymphocytes.

title: HSV-1 vs HSV-2?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HSV-1 vs HSV-2?
body.back: HSV-1: oral, eye, brain (childhood). HSV-2: genital, neonatal (sexual).

title: Features of HSV encephalitis?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Features of HSV encephalitis?
body.back: Necrotising, haemorrhagic, temporal; >70% mortality untreated; give aciclovir urgently.

title: VZV diseases?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: VZV diseases?
body.back: Chickenpox (primary), shingles (reactivation in a dermatome).

title: EBV diseases?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: EBV diseases?
body.back: Mononucleosis; Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lymphomas.

title: Herpes antivirals?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Herpes antivirals?
body.back: Aciclovir, valaciclovir; foscarnet, cidofovir if resistant; ganciclovir for CMV.

title: Herpes vaccines?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Herpes vaccines?
body.back: Varicella (live, 2 doses); shingles from 50 (Zostavax live, Shingrix subunit).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Invasive cervical cancer. Develops over 7-30 years after infection, which leaves a long window for screening.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CIN 1. Low-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: virus production, koilocytes; about half regress.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CIN 2/3. High-grade lesions with viral transformation (E6 and E7 oncoproteins), the true precursors of cancer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clearance. The immune system clears most infections within one to two years.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: HPV infection. Sexually transmitted infection of the cervical transformation zone; types 16 and 18 cause most cancers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Screening. Cytology (Pap smear) and HPV DNA testing find precancerous lesions that can be removed.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vaccination. L1 protein self-assembles into virus-like particles; vaccines protect before exposure.

title: HPV structure?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HPV structure?
body.back: Naked, icosahedral, 45-55 nm, circular dsDNA.

title: High vs low risk types?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: High vs low risk types?

title: Natural history to cancer?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Natural history to cancer?
body.back: Infection → CIN 1 → CIN 2/3 → invasive cancer over 7-30 years.

title: Screening methods?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Screening methods?
body.back: Pap smear cytology and HPV DNA testing.

title: HPV vaccines?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HPV vaccines?
body.back: VLPs of L1: bivalent (16, 18), quadrivalent (+6, 11), nonavalent (+31, 33, 45, 52, 58).

title: Who linked HPV and cervical cancer?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Who linked HPV and cervical cancer?
body.back: Harald zur Hausen (Nobel 2008).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Assembly. Virions are assembled from preformed parts; they do not grow or divide.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Attachment. A viral surface protein binds a specific cellular receptor: this defines tropism (susceptibility).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Penetration. Entry by membrane fusion (enveloped viruses) or endocytosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Release. Enveloped viruses bud through a membrane and take their envelope; naked viruses often lyse the cell.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Genome replication. Using viral enzymes (RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase) and host machinery; a permissive cell supplies the needed factors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Protein synthesis. Viral mRNAs are translated on host ribosomes: structural and non-structural proteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Uncoating. The capsid is removed and the genome is freed in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

title: Definition of a virus?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Definition of a virus?
body.back: Submicroscopic obligate intracellular parasite with one type of nucleic acid, assembled from parts.

title: Virion structure?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Virion structure?
body.back: Genome + capsid (capsomeres) = nucleocapsid, ± lipid envelope with glycoproteins.

title: Three classical criteria of classification?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Three classical criteria of classification?
body.back: Nucleic acid type, capsid symmetry, envelope.

title: Naked viruses?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Naked viruses?
body.back: DNA: parvo, adeno, papilloma. RNA: picornaviruses, HAV, HEV.

title: Baltimore classes?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Baltimore classes?
body.back: I dsDNA, II ssDNA, III dsRNA, IV +ssRNA, V −ssRNA, VI RNA-RT, VII DNA-RT.

title: Seven stages of the life cycle?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Seven stages of the life cycle?
body.back: Attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, synthesis, assembly, release.

title: Susceptibility vs permissiveness?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Susceptibility vs permissiveness?
body.back: Susceptible: has the receptor. Permissive: supports complete replication.

title: Oncogenic viruses?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Oncogenic viruses?
body.back: HPV, HBV, HCV, EBV, HHV-8, HTLV-1.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antigenic drift. Gradual change in HA and NA lets the virus partly escape existing immunity, causing yearly epidemics.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reassortment. When two strains infect the same cell (often in pigs), whole segments are exchanged.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Point mutations. The error-prone polymerase introduces mutations, mostly in the HA gene.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Segmented genome. Influenza A has 8 segments of negative-sense RNA; the envelope carries haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antigenic shift. A new HA and/or NA subtype to which humans have no immunity: pandemics (1918, 1957, 1968, 2009).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Annual vaccine. Composition is updated each year on WHO surveillance data, so vaccination must be repeated every autumn.

title: Influenza virus structure?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Influenza virus structure?
body.back: Enveloped, (−)ssRNA, 8 segments, HA, NA and M2.

title: Drift vs shift?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Drift vs shift?
body.back: Drift: point mutations → epidemics. Shift: reassortment → new subtype → pandemic.

title: Four major flu pandemics?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Four major flu pandemics?

title: Influenza treatment?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Influenza treatment?
body.back: Supportive (no aspirin in children); oseltamivir or zanamivir within 48 h.

title: Measles clinical picture?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Measles clinical picture?
body.back: Prodrome (3 C's + fever), Koplik spots, face-to-body rash.

title: Measles complications?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Measles complications?
body.back: Pneumonia, encephalitis (1/1000), giant cell pneumonia, SSPE (years later).

title: RSV disease and prevention?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: RSV disease and prevention?
body.back: Infant bronchiolitis; maternal vaccine 32-36 weeks or infant monoclonal antibody.

title: Parainfluenza types?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Parainfluenza types?
body.back: 1 and 2: croup. 3: bronchiolitis, pneumonia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Exposure. Any contact with an animal that may be rabid must be assessed immediately; there is no test before symptoms.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Category I. Touching or feeding the animal, licks on intact skin: no exposure.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Category II. Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding: exposure.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Category III. Single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, saliva on mucosa or broken skin, any direct contact with bats: severe exposure.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vaccine + RIG. Wound care, vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin (or monoclonal antibodies) infiltrated into the wound.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vaccination. Wound washing for at least 15 minutes with soap and water, then an immediate course of rabies vaccine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Washing only. Wash the exposed skin; no vaccine needed.

title: Rabies virus features?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Rabies virus features?
body.back: Rhabdoviridae, Lyssavirus; bullet-shaped, enveloped, (−)ssRNA; proteins G, N, M, P, L.

title: Main reservoir and vector?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Main reservoir and vector?
body.back: Dogs (~99% of human cases); bats in the Americas.

title: Two clinical forms?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Two clinical forms?
body.back: Furious (hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation) and paralytic (~20%).

title: Components of PEP?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Components of PEP?
body.back: Wound washing 15 min, vaccine course, immunoglobulin if category III.

title: WHO exposure categories?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: WHO exposure categories?
body.back: I: no exposure; II: minor, vaccine; III: severe, vaccine + immunoglobulin.

title: PEP schedules in Morocco?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: PEP schedules in Morocco?
body.back: Essen: days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28. Zagreb: 2 doses day 0, then 7 and 21.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Attachment. Envelope gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor, CCR5 (R5 strains) or CXCR4 (X4 strains); this defines tropism.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immune decline. Progressive loss of CD4 T cells; below 200/mm³ opportunistic infections and tumours define AIDS.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fusion. gp41 drives fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane (target of fusion and entry inhibitors).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Integration. Integrase inserts the viral DNA into the host chromosome as a provirus, which persists for the life of the cell (target of integrase inhibitors).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Assembly and maturation. Virions bud from the membrane; viral protease cleaves Gag-Pol so the particle becomes infectious (target of protease inhibitors).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reverse transcription. Reverse transcriptase copies the RNA genome into DNA; it is error-prone, generating great variability (target of NRTIs and NNRTIs).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Viral gene expression. Host RNA polymerase transcribes the provirus; Tat and Rev regulate expression; Gag, Pol and Env are made.

title: Retrovirus defining features?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Retrovirus defining features?
body.back: Enveloped, 2 × (+)ssRNA, reverse transcriptase, integration.

title: Three main HIV genes?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Three main HIV genes?
body.back: gag (structure, p24), pol (RT, integrase, protease), env (gp120, gp41).

title: HIV receptors?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HIV receptors?
body.back: CD4 + CCR5 or CXCR4.

title: HIV-1 vs HIV-2?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HIV-1 vs HIV-2?
body.back: HIV-1: global, more virulent. HIV-2: West Africa, less transmissible, milder.

title: Stages of HIV infection?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Stages of HIV infection?
body.back: Primary infection, asymptomatic (active) phase, minor symptoms, AIDS.

title: Early HIV tests?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Early HIV tests?
body.back: p24 antigen and HIV RNA; antibodies from 2-3 weeks.

title: How is HIV monitored?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: How is HIV monitored?
body.back: Viral load (PCR) and CD4 count (flow cytometry) every 3-6 months.

title: HTLV-1 diseases?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: HTLV-1 diseases?
body.back: Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma and HAM/TSP.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Entry inhibitors. Block attachment or fusion: enfuvirtide (HIV gp41), maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Integration. Integrase inhibitors (e.g. dolutegravir) stop HIV DNA from inserting into the host genome.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nucleic acid synthesis. The largest group: nucleoside analogues (aciclovir, ganciclovir), HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitors, HBV analogues, HCV polymerase inhibitors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Protein processing. Protease inhibitors for HIV and HCV prevent cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional proteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Release. Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir) trap new influenza virions on the cell surface.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Uncoating. Amantadine blocked the influenza A M2 channel; now little used because of resistance.

title: Types of viral vaccine?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Types of viral vaccine?
body.back: Live attenuated, inactivated, subunit/split, recombinant, VLP, viral vector, mRNA.

title: Examples of live viral vaccines?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Examples of live viral vaccines?
body.back: MMR, varicella, yellow fever, oral polio, rotavirus.

title: Contraindications to live vaccines?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Contraindications to live vaccines?
body.back: Pregnancy and immunodeficiency.

title: Active vs passive immunisation?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Active vs passive immunisation?
body.back: Active: own immune response, lasting. Passive: donated antibodies, immediate, ~4 months.

title: Why are antivirals hard to develop?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Why are antivirals hard to develop?
body.back: Viruses use host machinery → poor selectivity, toxicity.

title: Antiviral landmarks?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Antiviral landmarks?
body.back: Aciclovir 1983, AZT 1990, HAART mid-1990s, HCV DAAs 2011.

title: Five antiviral targets?
subject: subj:viro1

body.front: Five antiviral targets?
body.back: Entry, nucleic acid synthesis, protein processing, assembly, release.
